content_html:
Conceptual Metaphor Theory

Conceptual Metaphor Theory proposes that we understand abstract domains (time, causality, mathematics, morality) by mapping them from concrete, embodied source domains (space, motion, force, balance, containment). These mappings are systematic and support reasoning—not just language.

This diagram separates the process into three steps: embodied source schemas, a mapping operation, and abstract target domains. The examples show how a bodily pattern supplies the structure for abstract reasoning.

How metaphors organise memory and reasoning

Embodied schemas

  • Containment, path, balance, force are reused for abstract inference.
  • They provide intuitive “handles” for complex systems.

Contextual indexing

  • Metaphors become stable retrieval cues (e.g., “journey” for projects).
  • Colour/space tags reduce interference between concepts.

Neural reuse

  • Sensorimotor circuits activate during metaphor processing.
  • Parietal & premotor areas support spatialised thought.

Design your own metaphor set

  1. Select 3–5 embodied schemas that “fit” your domain (path, container, force).
  2. Define target-domain roles (goals, obstacles, resources, constraints).
  3. Choose colours for affect/salience (e.g., red = constraint; blue = generality).
  4. Sketch a proof/story path using these roles and rehearse spatially.
  5. Version and refine; swap schemas if they mislead or overconstrain.
